newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Azeris dismiss Turkmen claims to Caspian field.
newsitem.headline: Azeris dismiss Turkmen claims to Caspian field.

text.p: Azerbaijan on Tuesday dismissed Turkmenistan's claims to an oilfield the Azeris plan to develop in the Caspian Sea, and said that as far as it knew its two Russian partners in the project had not pulled out.

"The Kyapaz field is located in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea and any pretentions to the field are not based on international grounds," said a statement faxed to Reuters from Azerbaijan's state oil company, SOCAR.

Earlier this month, Turkmenistan demanded that a $1 billion preliminary deal between SOCAR, Russian state oil firm Rosneft and LUKoil to develop the Kyapaz field be anulled, arguing the field belongs to Turkmenistan.
Rosneft has said it would pull out in the wake of the Turkmen claim, while LUKoil's position remains unclear.
SOCAR said it had received no written confirmation that either Rosneft or LUKoil had abandoned the project.
"It should be noted that SOCAR has received no written documents about the unilateral annulment of this agreement from its Russian parters," the statement said.
The deposit is estimated to contain over 50 million tonnes of recoverable oil. Under the deal, SOCAR was to get 50 percent of the project, LUKoil 30 percent and Rosneft 20 percent.

Turkmenistan calls Kyapaz "Serdar". It also claims the Azeri-named Azeri field and part of the Chirag field, already under development by a multinational consortium headed by British Petroleum Co Plc and Norway's Statoil.

The SOCAR statement said Azerbaijan's rights to Kyapaz were established as early as 1959 when it was a republic of the now defunct Soviet Union, and were reaffirmed in 1970 by the Soviet ministry of oil and gas.
"(Kyapaz) was discovered in 1959 by Azeri geologists," said the statement, adding that in 1988 the site first began oil production.
"After the break up of the Soviet Union in 1991, SOCAR has held to the demarcation in 1970 by the Ministry of Oil and Gas of the USSR of the Caspian Sea into sectors.
"In all its official documents and in those of other competent organs of the USSR the Azeri, Turkmen, Kazakh and Russian sectors of the Caspian are clearly shown," it said.
The Caspian's legal status is the subject of intense diplomatic wrangling between the five states around its shores and oil majors wanting to cash in on the reserves.
The dispute hinges on whether, under international law, the Caspian is a sea or a lake. On that depends how national frontiers are drawn.

Moscow has argued that the Caspian is a salt lake whose oil resources should be developed jointly by the surrounding states. Others have said it is a sea which should be divided up between Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan.
